title: Deferred execution and hot-path traps (plan vs run)
hook: Declaring a LINQ query stores a plan, not results. Each time you enumerate — foreach, Count, ToList — the plan re-runs against the current source. On a busy submit path, that double pass can return different data.

blocks.text: Deferred execution means a LINQ query does not run when you assign it to a variable. It runs when you enumerate it or call an immediate operator. Immediate operators — Count, Any, First, Max, Sum, ToList, ToArray — execute right away. Deferred operators that return IEnumerable typically split into two classes: streaming (Where, Select, SelectMany, Take) yield elements as they read, and buffering (OrderBy, GroupBy, Reverse) read the entire source before yielding the first element.

entries.plainDefinition: The query is a recipe stored in an IEnumerable. Work happens only when you enumerate or materialize.
entries.example: var q = items.Where(x => x.Active); // no work yet

entries.plainDefinition: Operators that return a scalar or a concrete collection run the query right away.
Freezing a deferred query into a List or array with ToList or ToArray.
entries.example: var snapshot = query.ToList(); // one pass, reusable

entries.plainDefinition: Running the same IEnumerable plan more than once. Each pass re-executes all deferred operators.
entries.example: var c = q.Count(); foreach (var x in q) { } // two passes

blocks.text: On a high-concurrency submit path, enumerating the same filtered query twice is two CPU passes and potentially two different snapshots if the underlying list is still growing. Count then foreach on the same IEnumerable is the classic production bug. Chaining two Where clauses is still one pass when you finally enumerate, but calling ToList in the middle creates a second pass on a copy. Captured variables (cutoff, tenantId) are read at enumeration time, not at query construction — a race if those locals change between passes.

blocks.title: Hot-path fix
blocks.body: Call ToList once to snapshot, then share the list. One pass, one consistent view of the data.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Build the query
items.body: Assign a chain of Where/Select to a variable. No elements are read from the source.

items.title: First enumeration
items.body: Count() or foreach walks the source through the filter. If the source changed, results reflect the new state.

items.title: Second enumeration
items.body: Another foreach or Count re-runs the entire plan. Two passes, potentially different results.

items.title: Snapshot with ToList
items.body: ToList runs the plan once and stores results. Subsequent operations use the frozen list.

diagram.title: Deferred vs immediate operators
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  Q[Query variable\nstores plan] --> D{Enumerate?}
  D -->|No| W[No work done]
  D -->|foreach / ToList| E[Execute plan]
  E --> S{Operator type}
  S -->|Where Select Take| ST[Stream elements]
  S -->|OrderBy GroupBy| BU[Buffer all first]
  E --> M[Count First Max\nImmediate scalar]

snippet.label: Double enumeration on a live submit buffer
snippet.explanation: Count and foreach each run Where independently. Inserts between them change the report. ToList once is the hot-path fix.

snippet.label: Captured variable read at enumeration time
snippet.explanation: The lambda closes over minScore by reference. The value at enumeration time is what matters. Snapshot locals if you need a fixed threshold.

snippet.label: Loop variable capture in deferred queries
snippet.explanation: Closing over a for-loop iterator variable captures the variable, not the value. Copy to a local inside the loop body before using it in a lambda.

rows: Each filter creates a new array once
Spreading a generator twice re-runs it

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Calling Count then foreach on the same IEnumerable. Returning a query over a using-disposed enumerator (yield after dispose). Putting expensive Select lambdas in a query that reporting enumerates three times. Assuming OrderBy streams — it buffers the entire source first.

interviewTakeaways: Declaration is a plan; enumeration is work.
Scalar operators and ToList/ToArray are immediate; most sequence operators defer.
GroupBy/OrderBy defer but buffer; they are not cheap streaming.
Enumerate once on hot paths; snapshot captured filters.
commonPitfalls: Calling Count then foreach on the same IEnumerable.
Returning a query over a using-disposed enumerator (yield after dispose).
Putting expensive Select lambdas in a query that reporting enumerates three times.

jsTsCorrelations.note: array.filter is eager. JS iterators and generator pipelines are the deferred analogue. LINQ to Objects is closer to a generator chain than to Array.prototype.
A JS generator is lazy like IEnumerable until you spread it. Spreading twice re-runs the generator if you still have it.
